0.headline: IPO Action Returns: 3 public issues worth over Rs 10,000 crore to open next week
0.heading: IPO Action Returns: 3 public issues worth over Rs 10,000 crore to open next week
0.intro: The lineup comprises two mainboard initial public offerings and one SME issue.
0.body:
After a relatively quiet two-week period, partly due to the Diwali holidays, the primary market is set to regain momentum, with three IPOs worth more than Rs 10,000 crore scheduled to hit Dalal Street next week, starting November 16.

The lineup comprises two mainboard initial public offerings (IPOs) and one SME issue.

International Finance Corporation-backed agrochemicals and seeds company Crystal Crop Protection will be the first to launch its public issue, which will open for subscription on November 18. The company has fixed a price band of Rs 259-272 per share.

The New Delhi-headquartered crop protection solutions provider aims to raise Rs 455.7 crore through the IPO at a valuation of Rs 4,438.1 crore at the upper end of the price band. The offer comprises a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 355 crore, while promoter Ankur Aggarwal will offload shares worth Rs 100.7 crore through an offer for sale (OFS) of 37.02 lakh equity shares.

The net proceeds from the fresh issue will be primarily utilised to repay debt worth Rs 270 crore, against total outstanding borrowings of Rs 962.6 crore as of August 2026. The remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes.

The second mainboard IPO will be that of Mahanadi Coalfields, which is expected to raise around Rs 9,500 crore. The Coal India subsidiary will open its maiden public issue for subscription on November 19 and close it on November 23.

The IPO comprises an OFS of 66.18 crore equity shares by promoter Coal India, representing 10 percent of Mahanadi Coalfields' total paid-up equity capital.

Click Here To Read All IPO News

The entire proceeds from the offer, excluding issue expenses, will go to Coal India, the selling shareholder, while Mahanadi Coalfields will not receive any funds from the IPO.

SME company Watrana Rentals will also open its public issue on November 19. The company has fixed a price band of Rs 232-245 per share.

The Delhi-based material handling equipment provider aims to raise Rs 120 crore through its IPO at the upper end of the price band. The offer comprises an entirely fresh issue of 49.02 lakh equity shares.

Watrana Rentals plans to utilise Rs 98.12 crore of the IPO proceeds to purchase material handling equipment, aerial work platforms and batteries. The remaining funds will be used for general corporate purposes and offer-related expenses.

Meanwhile, a total of 303 companies, including 109 in the mainboard segment, launched their IPOs during the January-October period of 2026. The companies collectively raised Rs 1.66 lakh crore, of which mainboard IPOs accounted for more than Rs 1.57 lakh crore.

1.headline: Coal India arm Mahanadi Coalfields IPO to hit Dalal Street on November 19
1.heading: Coal India arm Mahanadi Coalfields IPO to hit Dalal Street on November 19
1.intro: Mahanadi Coalfields IPO | The public issue comprises an offer for sale of 66.18 crore equity shares by promoter Coal India, representing 10 percent of Mahanadi Coalfields' total paid-up equity capital.
1.body:
Mahanadi Coalfields, a subsidiary of the country's largest coal mining company, Coal India, will open its initial public offering (IPO) for public subscription on November 19. This will be the second mainboard IPO to open next week, alongside that of Crystal Crop Protection.

The IPO comprises an offer for sale (OFS) of 66.18 crore equity shares by promoter Coal India, representing 10 percent of Mahanadi Coalfields' total paid-up equity capital.

As a result, the entire proceeds from the offer, excluding issue expenses, will go to the selling shareholder, Coal India, and the company will not receive any funds from the IPO.

Moneycontrol was the first to report that Mahanadi Coalfields was likely to launch its maiden public offering next week, with the issue size expected to be around $1 billion, or approximately Rs 9,500 crore.

IPO Schedule

The one-day anchor book will open on November 18 for institutional investors, while the IPO will close for public subscription on November 23.

The share allotment is likely to be finalised on November 25, and Mahanadi Coalfields shares are scheduled to list on the stock exchanges on November 27.

Mahanadi Coalfields will be the third Coal India subsidiary to get listed on the stock exchanges, after Bharat Coking Coal and Central Mine Planning &amp; Design Institute.

The country's largest coal-producing company has reserved 3.3 crore equity shares, or 5 percent of the offer size, for its employees and 6.61 crore shares, or 10 percent of the total offer, for Coal India shareholders.

Click Here To Read All IPO News

Of the net offer, excluding the portions reserved for employees and shareholders, 50 percent has been earmarked for qualified institutional buyers (QIBs), 15 percent for non-institutional investors (NIIs), and the remaining 35 percent for retail investors.

Business

Mahanadi Coalfields was incorporated in April 1992 after being carved out of South Eastern Coalfields to meet the country's growing energy requirements by increasing coal production from two coalfields — Talcher and Ib Valley — in Odisha. These coalfields have estimated coal resources of approximately 106.76 billion tonnes.

Click Here To Read All IPO News

It is the largest coal producer among Coal India's subsidiaries, accounting for 28.4 percent of Coal India's total coal production in FY26 and 21 percent of domestic coal production. Its resources predominantly comprise thermal-grade non-coking coal.

Financial Performance

Mahanadi Coalfields reported a 6.7 percent year-on-year increase in profit to Rs 4,880.7 crore for the six months ended September 2026. Revenue rose 9.3 percent to Rs 16,093 crore during the same period compared with the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year.

For the financial year ended March 2026, however, profit declined 1.2 percent to Rs 10,698.1 crore, while revenue fell 2.6 percent to Rs 30,549.6 crore compared with the previous year.

SBI Capital Markets, Axis Capital, BOB Capital Markets, IDBI Capital Markets &amp; Securities, and IIFL Capital Services have been appointed as merchant bankers to the Mahanadi Coalfields IPO.

2.headline: Public listing may change 'Tata way', put profits ahead of philanthropy: Noel Tata
2.heading: Public listing may change 'Tata way', put profits ahead of philanthropy: Noel Tata
2.intro: He said Tata Trusts would work with regulators and other stakeholders to find a solution that preserves the group's founding ethos.
2.body:
Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata on Saturday expressed concern that a proposed public listing of Tata Sons could fundamentally alter the group's traditional business philosophy, warning that a wider shareholder base may eventually place profits ahead of philanthropy.

"My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way. And one day, if we have 30,000-40,000 shareholders, profit may take precedence over philanthropy. And I think that will fundamentally change the Tata way of working," Noel Tata said at the HT Leadership Summit 2026.

He said Tata Trusts would work with regulators and other stakeholders to find a solution that preserves the group's founding ethos.

"Tata Trusts will play a constructive role with regulators and others to try and find a solution which keeps the Tata way the way it is," he said.

The remarks come against the backdrop of an intensifying tussle between Tata Trusts and the Tata Sons board over the holding company's ownership structure and leadership.

Tata Trusts, which controls about 66 per cent of Tata Sons - the holding company of the USD 165 billion Tata Group - has opposed a public listing, while the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, its second-largest shareholder with an 18.37 per cent stake, has backed a stock market float to unlock value from its investment.

The dispute gained momentum after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rejected Tata Sons' September 2026 application to surrender its registration as a core investment company, effectively closing a route the group had pursued to avoid mandatory listing as an upper-layer non-banking financial company.

At a September 17 board meeting, Tata Sons decided to initiate steps towards listing in line with RBI regulations and approved a fresh five-year term for Chairman N Chandrasekaran, reversing his August decision not to seek reappointment after February 2027.

Noel Tata opposed both decisions, with the Trusts subsequently questioning the legality of Chandrasekaran's reappointment. The board approved his reappointment by a 4:1 vote.

Emphasising continuity in the group's philosophy, Noel on Saturday said its ownership structure and institutional character had helped preserve its values across generations.

"The owner cannot die, the owner cannot be bought and the owner cannot retire. There is continuity in what happens the Tata way," he said.

The group has historically combined commercial operations with philanthropy and nation-building, with Tata Trusts playing a central role in its institutional framework.

On the group's strategic direction, Noel said there was no question about its broad objectives, but greater discipline was needed in executing large projects and allocating capital.

"Philanthropy on one hand. Nation building on the other. This is independence of leadership and personalities and this will continue. I do not question the direction of what we have done. I question, sometimes, the delivery of what we are doing," he said.

"The question is, do we have the discipline when we execute projects, and not the direction? How will projects with a long gestation period succeed if we don't have discipline? And how will we allocate capital to those projects?" he said.

"So, very clearly, the direction is fine, but we also need discipline in the execution of these very large projects," he added.

Highlighting the group's role in India's industrial development, Noel said Tata companies were participating in emerging sectors such as semiconductors and electric vehicle batteries.

"We are partners in India's development," he said, adding that the group was undertaking its first semiconductor project and setting up its first EV battery plant.

Noel also spoke about the growth of Tata's retail business, particularly Trent, which operates the Westside and Zudio brands.

He said Zudio was launched in 2016 to cater to consumers at the bottom of the economic pyramid by offering aspirational products at affordable prices.

"It was not that this aspiration for better product was only in the top metros or with the wealthy. The aspiration went down all the way. So we said, how can we address in a way the bottom of the pyramid? So in 2016, we launched Zudio to address this bottom of the pyramid with an aspirational product," he said.

The format started with air-conditioned stores of around 6,000 square feet, with prices beginning at Rs 199, he said, adding that the starting price point had remained unchanged over the past decade.

On Westside, Noel said the decision to adopt a private-label model gave the company control over the entire value chain, from fabric and product design to retailing.

He said Westside, which began with doubts over whether such a retail format could succeed in India, now operated around 320 stores and was looking at expanding to more than 500.

Attributing the growth partly to rising consumption, he said demand had increased across socio-economic categories and markets over the past decade.

Noel also said the opportunity to address the needs of underserved sections of society had made a deep impression on him after taking over as chairman of Tata Trusts, adding that the experience had given him greater humility about the scale of social challenges in India.

Tata Trusts vice-chairman Venu Srinivasan and other trustees backing a stock market listing of Tata Sons are understood to favour greater transparency, stronger corporate governance and a clearer ownership structure for India's largest business conglomerate.

They argue that listing would subject the holding company to greater public and regulatory scrutiny, institutionalise decision-making and reduce uncertainty over succession and governance in a group whose businesses span multiple sectors. A public listing could also provide a market-determined valuation of Tata Sons and give investors greater visibility into the financial and strategic decisions of the group.

In a November 11 letter to fellow trustee Darius Khambata, Srinivasan and fellow vice-chairman Vijay Singh cited examples such as Novo Nordisk, Hershey, Lundbeck and Demant to argue that companies can remain anchored by charitable foundations while being publicly traded.

They also pointed to listed Tata companies, including TCS, Tata Steel, Tata Power and Tata Motors, which have undertaken long-gestation investments and nation-building projects without compromising their institutional character.

The Trusts would continue to retain their shareholding in Tata Sons and receive dividends to fund philanthropic activities, they argued, adding that greater disclosure would bring discipline rather than constrain the group's long-term ambitions.
